THOUGHT: This 3-year-old boy presents with a classic triad of recurrent pyogenic infections (skin abscesses, respiratory infections), granulomatous inflammation (persistent skin lesions, lymphadenopathy), and failure to thrive — all beginning in early infancy (since 2 months old). The presence of pus-producing skin lesions, cervical/axillary lymphadenopathy, and recurrent fevers suggests chronic, poorly controlled bacterial and possibly fungal infections. Laboratory findings show neutrophilia with left shift (indicating ongoing infection/inflammation), normal hemoglobin and platelets (arguing against bone marrow failure or leukemia), and — critically — an abnormal Nitroblue Tetrazolium (NBT) test and decreased neutrophil oxidative burst. The NBT test assesses the ability of phagocytes (especially neutrophils) to generate superoxide via the NADPH oxidase complex; an abnormal result indicates defective respiratory burst, hallmark of chronic granulomatous disease (CGD). CGD is an X-linked or autosomal recessive primary immunodeficiency characterized by inability to kill catalase-positive organisms (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus, Serratia marcescens, Burkholderia cepacia, Aspergillus spp.), leading to recurrent abscesses, granuloma formation, lymphadenitis, and inflammatory complications (e.g., colitis, obstructive granulomas). Failure to thrive reflects chronic inflammation and recurrent infection burden. The age of onset (<6 months), pattern of infections, physical findings (lymphadenopathy, indolent skin lesions), and confirmatory functional testing (abnormal NBT, decreased oxidative burst) strongly support CGD over other immunodeficiencies (e.g., severe combined immunodeficiency would present with severe viral/fungal infections and profound lymphopenia; hyper-IgE syndrome features eczema, staph abscesses, and elevated IgE but preserved oxidative burst; leukocyte adhesion deficiency would show marked neutrophilia without tissue infiltration, and normal NBT).

DIAGNOSIS: Chronic Granulomatous Disease
